en: Not deceive you with some clever trick;
May that swine whose home burned
Not butcher us in this way!
May unmitigated disaster not race
To Chinmachin and Beijing;
May Karagul, doomed to die in flames,
Not send word in every direction.
He was a deceiver, a consummate trickster,
One of the most resourceful slaves.
Be wary of Karagul,
My beloved champion!
If the troublesome slave falls into your hands,
Gouge out his eyes until they are blinded;
If he begs, do not spare his life—
Seize him and kill him.
Put the swine who thwarted your desire
To a complete end!
Karagul, son of Katal—
Here is the dark peril!
He is an obsequious slave;
My colt, my son, listen well:
He is one of our true enemies!
A slave skilled among spearmen,
A foremost slave, ingenious in stratagems!
That is the accursed man himself;
He became khan of the horse herders,
And, unless what I say is false,
This is the time when he lives in luxury.
When one fancy takes him,
He eats the frozen fat of an ox;
When another fancy takes him,
He eats the suckling foal of a barren mare.
This year God must have struck the slave;
He gives no thought to anything,
Growing violent from drinking spirits,
Growing heated from drinking koumiss,
With sweat streaming down to his bones.
Karagul must have become such a creature;
Karagul must have become a khan
As great as a mountain among the horse herders.
Gray must now streak his beard;
That swine, like me,
Must have become a hoary old man.
Once he is parted from his bay stallion,
If you do not destroy his black racer Kyydu,
You will witness
The turmoil Karagul brings!
I have said much—heed my words;
My precious child, understand!
At the edge of the horse herds,
On the face of Kürpüldök,
In the hollow of Kyr-Kayyn,
Along the sickle-shaped ridge,
Karagul’s tent
Can be seen standing right there,
Along with the hero named Karagul.
He makes himself known;
From inside that tent,
The accursed swine
Makes his lordly rank known.
Four or five horse herders at a time
Carry him outside so he can urinate.
Karagul’s life of pleasure
Keeps the accursed dog alive.
Upon his wretched throne,
Whenever he raises his head,
The horse herders feed him
Slices of fatty meat.
That is the accursed man himself—
I have described his measure in this way;
That is the look of Karagul!
How much have I told you of Karagul,
And of the multitude of horses,
Swarming like ants, that are his!
His geldings outnumber his stallions;
His herd contains every kind:
Mottled roans and blaze-faced horses;
That swine’s herd
Mixes argamaks and thoroughbreds.
It has bracelet-marked gray horses,
And untouched horses that have never been ridden.
Among those herds
Are wondrous animal coursers,
And even Kambar-Ata is there.
That swine Karagul will not leave his horses;
While Karagul remains alive,
Your undertaking will not prosper!
Wondrous creatures, the finest of livestock—
Kongurbai’s countless horses
Are all consummate coursers.
There are horses with tails an armful thick;
He gathered the coursers with a clamor,
And the mighty one seized them all.
I have said much—understand;
My mighty orphan, heed my words!
I will tell you the road to take:
Sometimes visible, sometimes not,
The cursed place lies
Where the blue haze parts—
That is the desert where no living soul travels.
Drawing this way from there,
That is the lake of It-Ichpes.
Where the gray haze can be seen
Is the edge of Uzun-Too.
That is the mine where the Kara-Chinese
And the many Manchus dig gold.
When you reach that place
And turn to your left,
There is a gaping gorge.
Left behind by Manas, I, Bakai,
Tell many of my sorrows.
Yesterday, when the gray wolves went scouting,
When my champion Almam,
Called Saiypburush, went forth,
There was a pass called Tuman-Kyr;
Looking directly across from it,
There was a place called Madangshong.
That is where my noble gray wolf Alma
Pulled the reins and turned the head
Of the thoroughbred Aisarala;
That is where my dear elder brother measured
Hero Khan Kongurbai,
The infidel like a black worm,
And kept watch upon his sentry post!
When you reach that place,
My formidable one left by the hero,
Ride on along the road
And raise your spyglass to your eye!
Get sound intelligence
Of hero Khan Kongurbai,
Infidel son of Kaldai,
Who pastures at Chok-Tabylgy
And tethers his great black horse!
This year the mighty swine, khan of the Kechil—
The impetuous great Kongur—
Has taken command of the Manchu army
And is gathering it, I hear.
“How great has the valor become
Of the orphan son of Manas?”
Of everyone who comes and goes,
He goes about asking, I hear.
Beyond those horse herds,
On this side of the Sary-Suu,
Where seven rivers unite at their head,
There lies Kaldai’s Kara-Suu.
Honored orphan, heed my words:
There lies this dark peril!
From the far bank to the near bank,
Even a courser cannot sport across it;
As for the depth of that dark water,
Forty ropes lowered in cannot sound it.
This is the lay of the land;
My orphan, my son, listen well!
Go there and see it with your own eyes,
Saying, ‘Capable Bakai told me.’
He used to be lord of the land;
No wild ass escaped before his face,
And no kinsman of Kongurbai
Ever stirred a step before me.
This year Kongurbai must have scouted the road,
Wearing the flanks of his horses lean,
That swine whose home burned
Traveling every road
The ear had heard and the eye had seen.
Finding no enemy, he must have turned back;
That shambling swine must have spoken
His last instructions to Karagul,
Telling him to let them graze freely.
Kongurbai must have added Algara to the herd
And then returned,
And that doomed man must have told Karagul
The secret of his death!
My hawk born of Manas,
Do not go by day—go by night;
Raise a battle cry and seize the horses!
Drive his herd and bring it back.
If Karagul, son of Katal,
Should happen to fall into your hands,
Slaughter him as a sacrifice;
Cut off his head, fasten it securely,
And bring it to your uncle!
The road to Beijing is over there;
My valiant orphan, reconnoiter the road!
Store this old man’s words in your pack,
Saying, ‘My valiant uncle told me.’
Through gray haze and burning dust,
Judge the way and reconnoiter the road.
My champion, whom I beheld late in life,
Heed the words of your aged uncle,
An old man resembling a prophet!
Go straight into the dark mass of horses
And thrust out your spear;
Face the heedless slave’s herd
And raid and seize it!
Pour out your wrath, my only one,
And strike down his countless black livestock.
Ease the anguish held in the breast
Of your grieving uncle Bakai!
Let the horses scatter at your attack,
And let the fat ones be slaughtered;
Let every beast and predator
Feast upon them with a blessing!
Amen, my child, amen!
May the affair with China run its course;
May it become a deed the people
Will not forget until the end of days!
Scatter Kongurbai’s livestock;
Open wide as umach the eyes
Of your mole-marked uncle Bakai!
You have set out upon a perilous horse raid;
You have gone alone toward Beijing,
My only one, whom I beheld late in life—
I entrust you to the one God!
Raid and seize the horses
Of the teeming infidels;
One who spares an enemy will be wounded—
Cut down every horse herder
Without a moment’s hesitation!
May God prosper your undertaking;
My champion, whom I beheld late in life,
May your lion father Manas support you!
To the one creator God
I have commended you;
May your khan and uncle, now grown old,
See you return alive!
If you let yourself be overcome, calamity will follow;
To Allah Most High, Japar,
I now entrust you for safekeeping!”
His white beard grown sparse,
The tears of your uncle Bakai
Poured from his eyes;
He sobbed as he offered his blessing,
Your uncle trembling, unable to stand.
Spreading his hands and saying, “Amen!”
Bakai the holy sage strode forth,
Dedicating his prayer to the spirit
Of Manas, who had gone to the other world.
The splendid hero, the noble man’s son,
Felt Allah’s sun cloud over in the sky,
And sixty cares came upon him at once:
“If the moon is dark and troubled,
What will the night become?” he thought.
“If death overtakes me and I fall to a bullet,
What will become of the days
Of my uncle left behind me?” he thought.
The splendid hero, son of Manas,
Mounted thoughtfully, that valiant man,
His dear eyes, like a saker falcon’s,
Filling with tears without blinking.
Tormented that he had not gathered the people,
Formed an army, and brought it with him,
The young champion, the lion’s son,
Stood grieving and lamenting aloud.
Yet grieving was of no avail;
He had no choice but to go to the horses!
His eyes blazed like a lion’s;
